title: Light and Sound
description: Mirrors, music, and the wave patterns hiding in everyday sights and sounds.

questions.prompt: Which process lets you see your face in an ordinary mirror?
questions.hint: Light reaches your eyes after interacting with the surface.
questions.explanation: A mirror reflects light from your face back toward your eyes.

questions.prompt: What is a loudspeaker cone doing when it produces a steady tone?

choices.text: Changing air into a new gas

questions.hint: The disturbance in the air repeats regularly.
questions.explanation: The cone vibrates, producing alternating compressions and rarefactions in the surrounding air.

questions.prompt: Which property chiefly determines whether a pure musical tone sounds high or low?
questions.hint: Count how often the vibration repeats, not how large it is.
questions.explanation: A tone's pitch is chiefly related to its frequency; faster repetition produces a higher pitch.

The time the light spends outside the glass

questions.hint: The colors do not all change direction by the same amount.
questions.explanation: Dispersion occurs because the refractive index varies with wavelength, so different colors bend by different amounts.

questions.prompt: A straw looks bent where it enters water because light undergoes what?
questions.hint: The light crosses between materials in which it travels at different speeds.
questions.explanation: Refraction changes the direction of light at an angled boundary between air and water, shifting the apparent position of the submerged straw.

questions.prompt: A wave's frequency doubles while its speed remains unchanged. What happens to its wavelength?
questions.hint: Wave speed depends on both spacing and repetition rate.
questions.explanation: Speed equals frequency times wavelength. At fixed speed, doubling frequency halves wavelength.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Verified v=f times wavelength; fixed v implies wavelength inversely proportional to f.

questions.prompt: In an ordinary sound wave traveling through air, the air molecules oscillate mainly in which direction?

choices.text: In continuous circles around the source

questions.hint: Distinguish the motion of the disturbance from that of individual molecules.
questions.explanation: Sound in air is longitudinal: molecules oscillate back and forth parallel to the direction of wave propagation.

questions.prompt: Two equal-amplitude sound waves of the same frequency reach a point exactly half a cycle out of phase. Ideally, what happens there?
questions.hint: Add the instantaneous pressure variations at that point.
questions.explanation: Each wave's pressure variation cancels the other's when they are equal and opposite, giving ideal destructive interference.

questions.hint: The two ends impose different displacement conditions on the air.
questions.explanation: A displacement node at the closed end and antinode at the open end permit the fundamental and its odd harmonics.

questions.prompt: Two pure tones of 440 and 444 hertz sound together. What beat frequency do they produce?
questions.hint: The slow variation comes from how quickly the tones drift in and out of phase.
questions.explanation: The beat frequency is the absolute difference: 444 minus 440 equals 4 hertz.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Verified absolute frequency difference is 4 Hz, not mean/sum/half-difference.

questions.prompt: Ignoring absorption and reflections, you move from 2 meters to 4 meters from a point sound source radiating uniformly. Its intensity becomes what fraction?
questions.hint: The same power is spread over a larger spherical area.
questions.explanation: Intensity follows the inverse square of distance. Doubling the distance reduces it to one-quarter.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Verified (2/4) squared equals 1/4. Uniform point source, free-field assumptions explicit; asks intensity rather than perceived loudness.

questions.prompt: Unpolarized light passes through two ideal polarizers whose axes differ by 60 degrees. What fraction of the original intensity emerges?
questions.hint: Treat the first polarizer separately, then apply the angle-dependent transmission to the second.
questions.explanation: The first polarizer transmits half. The second transmits cos-squared 60 degrees, or one-quarter, of that half: one-eighth overall.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Verified Malus law: 1/2 times cos(60 degrees)^2 = 1/2 times 1/4 = 1/8. Input unpolarized and both polarizers ideal.

questions.prompt: For fixed monochromatic light and a distant screen, narrowing a single slit does what to its central diffraction maximum?

choices.text: Splits it into two equal central maxima

questions.hint: Compare aperture size with wavelength when locating the first dark fringes.
questions.explanation: The first minima satisfy slit width times sine of angle equals wavelength. A narrower slit therefore produces a wider central maximum.

questions.prompt: A two-slit light experiment is completely immersed in a transparent liquid of refractive index 1.5. Geometry and source frequency stay fixed. In the small-angle limit, fringe spacing becomes what fraction of its value in air?
questions.hint: Identify which wave property changes in the liquid, then use its role in fringe spacing.
questions.explanation: The wavelength in the liquid is divided by 1.5 while frequency stays fixed. Fringe spacing is proportional to wavelength, so it becomes two-thirds as large.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Verified spacing proportional to wavelength and wavelength_medium=wavelength_air/1.5 (air index approximated as 1), giving 2/3. Whole optical region immersed, unchanged geometry and small-angle limit explicit.
